rv.q: It is to the enormous credit of this small show staged in a time of recovery, that you’ll journey back across the landscape of your own life.
At these moments, the room itself seems to be crying, filled past bursting with weeping, laughing, explosive life.
Lackawanna Blues is, after all, a memory play, and Santiago-Hudson makes no bones about presenting the ghosts (and occasional monster) of his childhood with an enveloping and inviting compassion.
Ruben Santiago-Hudson’s solo show “Lackawanna Blues” still gleams like a newly minted coin some 20 years after it was first produced.
This maternal figure stands tall, talks truth, and envelops her little band of losers in the warming embrace of honest affection and genuine respect.
Ruben Santiago-Hudson’s autobiographical solo is a gentle and generous tribute to the staunch woman who raised him.
It always comes back to Nanny, with her stiff back and neatly folded arms; Santiago-Hudson's rendering evokes a Cicely Tyson type, a strong Black matriarch not to be trifled with.
As actor-writer, director, impersonator, harmonica player, he excels.
Lackawanna Blues is not to be missed.
That spark is what makes Lackawanna probably the most honest show in New York right now: 90 minutes of earnest, unsentimental love for one’s past.
Lackawanna Blues is a beautiful testament to their relationship, and the wider community surrounding it.

The writing, which is more a series of scattered anecdotes and memories than a traditional narrative, mixes retelling the characters’ sorrowful pasts with lively comic touches, leading to earnest character portraits that are affecting and involving.
Lackawanna Blues provides stirring evidence of how much Nanny did for Santiago-Hudson.
Santiago-Hudson brings all these people to life with remarkable physicality and magical changes of voice.
The miracle of this “Lackawanna Blues” is the absolute lack of effort Santiago-Hudson shows in switching from an adult woman to a little boy.

Yet, as engrossing as much of the show is -- and all of it is enhanced by the almost-constant background guitar-playing by Junior Mack of the music of the late, great Bill Sims Jr. -- I have to admit (somewhat sadly) that the piece didn’t fully satisfy me.
I want to urge everyone to see the show, which has just been extended through Nov. 12, because it's a good one.

cn.t: Santiago-Hudson delivers a virtuosic solo performance embodying dozens of characters from his childhood, though critics split on whether this tender, blues-infused memoir transcends the self-indulgent pitfalls of autobiographical storytelling.
